lesson.title: Collision Domains: Where CSMA/CD Actually Has Work to Do
lesson.summary: A collision domain is the set of devices whose transmissions can physically collide with each other on a shared medium, and it is the reason Ethernet's original CSMA/CD algorithm exists at all. Switches, by giving each device its own dedicated link, shrink a collision domain down to almost nothing.
lesson.body:
A collision domain is the set of devices that could have their transmissions physically interfere with one another because they share the same transmission medium. This was the central design constraint of original Ethernet, which ran over shared coaxial cable, and it remained true for Ethernet over hubs, since a hub simply repeats every electrical signal to every port. In a collision domain, if two devices transmit at the same moment, their signals combine on the wire and both transmissions are corrupted. Managing this problem, not eliminating it but detecting and recovering from it, was the whole job of the algorithm Ethernet was built around: CSMA/CD.

Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection breaks down into exactly what its name describes. Carrier sense means a device listens to the medium and only begins transmitting once it senses the line is idle. Multiple access acknowledges that many devices legitimately share that medium and have equal rights to use it. Collision detection happens after a device starts sending: it keeps monitoring the wire while transmitting, and if the signal it observes does not match what it is sending, another device transmitted at nearly the same instant and the two signals collided. When a collision is detected, the transmitting stations send a brief jam signal so every device on the segment recognizes it occurred, then each colliding station waits a random backoff interval, drawn from a range that grows with repeated collisions, before retransmitting.

A hub's ports all belong to a single collision domain, because the hub repeats one device's signal onto every wire simultaneously, so any two devices attached to it are always at risk of colliding if they transmit at the same time. A switch changes this completely. Because each switch port is its own dedicated, typically full duplex link, a device on one port can transmit at the exact same instant as a device on another port with zero chance of interference. On a genuinely full duplex link, sending and receiving even happen on separate wire pairs, so there is no shared medium left to contend for, and CSMA/CD has nothing to do; it is simply switched off.

Picture four PCs, A, B, C, and D, all connected to the same hub. A and C both sense the line idle at nearly the same instant and start transmitting to different destinations. Partway through, their signals collide on the shared medium; both detect the collision, send a jam signal, and back off for a random interval before retrying. Meanwhile B and D, sharing that same collision domain, could not have transmitted successfully during that window either, since the segment was occupied by the collision and its aftermath. Now replace the hub with a four port switch running full duplex. A and C can transmit to their destinations at the exact same instant with no possibility of collision, since each device sits on its own dedicated link rather than a shared one.

It is worth keeping collision domains and broadcast domains conceptually separate, even though both arose in the context of shared Ethernet hardware. A collision domain is about physical contention for a shared medium, a concern CSMA/CD exists to manage. A broadcast domain, covered in the previous chapter, is about how far a broadcast frame's address scope reaches, a concern only a router or VLAN can contain. A switch shrinks collision domains to essentially one device per port, which is why collisions are nearly extinct on modern wired networks, but a switch does nothing to shrink a broadcast domain: that requires a router or VLAN.
